title: Building a Cold Frame From Salvaged Windows
author: Ruth Okafor
date: 2026-04-12
extractor: trafilatura
---
Every spring I promise myself I will stop starting seedlings on the kitchen windowsill, and every spring the windowsill fills up anyway. This year I finally did something about it. A neighbour was replacing the sash windows on their terrace, and two of the old frames ended up leaning against my shed with a note that said take them, please.
## Planning the box
A cold frame is nothing more than a bottomless box with a transparent lid. The back should be taller than the front so that rain runs off and the low spring sun reaches the plants. I sized the box to the windows rather than the other way round, which is the single most useful piece of advice I can give anyone working with salvage.
- Two sash windows, roughly 90 by 60 centimetres each
- Four lengths of scaffold board from the skip behind the hardware shop
- A box of exterior screws and two pairs of hinges
The whole thing cost a little under twenty pounds, most of which went on the screws. If you have to buy timber, untreated larch is a good choice because it lasts for years without any preservative near your vegetables.
## Putting it together
I cut the side panels on a slope, screwed the boards to corner posts, and hinged the windows along the back edge. Old paint can contain lead, so I left it on and sealed it rather than sanding it off. A stick with notches cut into it props the lid open on warm afternoons; ventilation matters more than people expect, and seedlings can cook on a sunny day in April.
> The best cold frame is the one you can open with one hand while holding a watering can in the other.
Three weeks later, the frame is full of lettuce, chard and a tray of leeks that I am trying not to look at too often. The windowsill, for the first time in years, has nothing on it but a cactus.
